title: Indian-American Voters Take Centre Stage in Texas and New York Midterms
excerpt: A viral Texas early-vote post and a 500-strong Long Island rally for Tom Suozzi put turnout, not candidates, in focus
body:
• A second-generation Indian-American voter in Texas, Vasant Bhatt, drew about 857,000 views in seven hours after posting that he voted for Democrat James Talarico, citing xenophobia and racial resentment.
  • More than 500 Indian Americans rallied in Uniondale, New York, for Representative Tom Suozzi, whose Long Island district includes a sizeable Indian-American community.
  • The 2026 AAPI Voter Survey put Indian-American support for Democratic Senate candidates at 66-18, though the Indian-American sample was small.
  • Early voting is under way in Texas ahead of the November 3 midterms; New York early voting and turnout in Dallas-Fort Worth, Houston and Long Island suburbs are the next tests of outreach in Hindi, Gujarati and Telugu.

A single early vote in Texas has become one of the most visible moments of the midterm campaign for Indian-American voters. Vasant Bhatt, a second-generation Indian American, posted on X on Monday that he had cast his ballot for James Talarico, the Democratic nominee for the U.S. Senate in Texas. Within seven hours the post had about 857,000 views, 7,300 likes and 3,000 replies, according to reporting by IANS via hi INDiA.

“I just cast my ballot for James Talarico. As a second-generation Indian American, I am thoroughly disgusted by the xenophobia, racial resentment, and increasingly brazen attacks on my identity,” the post read. “My family has contributed to the American story through hard work, sacrifice, and an unwavering belief in the opportunities this nation promises. I am every bit as American as anyone else, and I will not tolerate being treated as a perpetual foreigner in the country I call home.”

"I am every bit as American as anyone else, and I will not tolerate being treated as a perpetual foreigner in the country I call home."

— Vasant Bhatt, second-generation Indian-American voter in Texas

Bhatt urged other eligible Texans to vote, framing the election as a defence of principles. The response was sharply divided. Conservative commentator Patrick Casey replied in a post that drew about 32,000 views and said Bhatt had once interned for Republican Senator Ted Cruz. That exchange, rather than any candidate speech, is what pulled national attention to the Texas race this week.

A different story from the candidate races

The Videshi has already covered Indian-American candidates on ballots from Texas to Florida as early voting opened. This development is about voters, not candidates. Bhatt is not running for office, and Representative Tom Suozzi, the focus of the New York mobilisation, is not Indian American. What links Texas and New York is organised community turnout in places where Indian Americans live in large numbers and where suburban margins are narrow.

Texas has one of the largest Indian-American populations in the country, concentrated in Dallas-Fort Worth and Houston. In New York, more than 500 Indian Americans gathered in Uniondale to back Suozzi’s re-election bid. Suozzi, a Democrat, represents New York’s 3rd District on Long Island. Community leader Varinder Bhalla compared Suozzi to former Representative Stephen Solarz, a longtime champion of ties with India in Congress.

What the numbers do and do not show

The 2026 AAPI Voter Survey found Indian-American voters backing Democratic Senate candidates by 66 to 18. Both reports carrying the survey result caution that its Indian-American sample is relatively small, so it should be read as a direction, not a precise forecast. The longer pattern is clearer: Indian Americans have historically leaned Democratic, and both parties are courting them this cycle.

Immigration and H-1B visa rhetoric has become a theme in several races, according to the IANS report. That context helps explain why a post framed around identity, rather than taxes or spending, travelled so far. Asian Americans are the fastest-growing group of eligible voters in the United States, and parties have run targeted outreach in Hindi, Gujarati and Telugu in suburban districts.

Why this matters for Indian-American readers

For families in Plano, Sugar Land, Edison-adjacent Long Island suburbs and similar communities, the practical question is not only who wins a Senate or House seat. It is whether campaign language on immigration and visas changes the climate at work, at school and in public life. Bhatt’s post named that concern directly. The Suozzi rally pointed the other way: a community rewarding a member of Congress it views as a consistent advocate on U.S.-India ties.

What’s next

Early voting continues in Texas ahead of the November 3 election, which will decide control of Congress. The test now is turnout. If the online attention around Bhatt’s post and the in-person turnout in Uniondale translate into early-vote numbers in Dallas-Fort Worth, Houston and Long Island, both parties will have evidence that their multilingual outreach worked. If they do not, the week will be remembered as a viral moment that did not move ballots.
